title: Showcase project: quiz night
prompt:
Your showcase project, option two. `quiz.py` runs a quiz from a question bank in `questions.json` (three fictional shop questions). Loading the bank and playing the game already work. Finish two functions:

`is_right(reply, answer)` is `True` when the reply matches the answer, ignoring capital letters and spaces at either end. `score(questions, replies)` counts how many replies are right.

When the tests pass, run `python3 quiz.py` and play. Then add a question of your own to `questions.json` and play again.
hints: Strings have a `lower()` method [py-160]. They also have `strip()`: try `"  Gear ".strip()` in the Python REPL to see what it does. Tidy both strings the same way before you compare them with `==`.
`is_right` can be one line: `return reply.strip().lower() == answer.strip().lower()`.
In `score`, start a counter at 0. Walk through the questions and the replies side by side with `zip(questions, replies)`, and add 1 each time `is_right(reply, item["a"])` is `True`.
explain_after:
Your quiz reads its questions with `json.load` [py-105], keeps each question as a small dictionary [py-082], and walks two lists side by side with `zip()` [py-107]. The last test plays a whole game: it starts `quiz.py` as a separate program and types three answers into it.

Adding a question needs no new code, only a new line in the JSON file. Keeping data apart from code like that is a habit worth keeping.
